Europe’s ammunition drive hits cotton supply bottleneck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:20:32 UTC
21:20:32 KST

155 mm N795 artillery projectiles are stored during manufacturing process. (AP photo)
Europe’s efforts to expand ammunition production are running into a shortage of cotton linters, a little-known raw material needed to manufacture propellants for artillery shells and other munitions.
Cotton linters are the short fibers left on cotton seeds after the longer fibers used by the textile industry have been removed. Once purified, their high cellulose content makes them suitable for producing nitrocellulose, the principal ingredient in smokeless propellants.
The propellant burns rapidly inside a weapon, generating the gas needed to launch a projectile. It is separate from the explosive charge carried by an artillery shell.
Demand has risen sharply since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, rapidly depleting European ammunition stocks. Production of NATO-standard 155 mm shells has increased, but shortages of nitrocellulose and other inputs have limited how quickly manufacturers can expand output.
The Wall Street Journal reported that limited linter supplies remained one of the main obstacles to NATO’s efforts to replenish its ammunition reserves. European nitrocellulose capacity would need to more than double to about 20,000 tons a year to meet projected demand, according to estimates cited by the newspaper.
Europe’s reliance on China has added to concerns over security of supply. Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger said in 2024 that European producers obtained more than 70 percent of their cotton linters from China.
The issue also has direct relevance for Türkiye, which produces both cotton and military-grade nitrocellulose.
The state-owned Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation’s (MKE) Powder Factory in the central province of Kırıkkale already manufactures several types of nitrocellulose and propellant powder for small- and large-caliber ammunition.
MKE is also building the Hüseyin Kâhya Energetic Materials Factory in Kırıkkale as part of its investment program covering 2023-2027. The facility is scheduled to begin production in 2026 and will manufacture nitrocellulose, gunpowder, rocket fuel, concentrated nitric acid and solid TNT.
The Defense Ministry has said the investment will approximately triple Türkiye’s existing production capacity for gunpowder, rocket fuel and explosives while reducing dependence on imported chemicals.
Türkiye’s cotton cultivation and processing industry could provide access to linter feedstock as European manufacturers seek alternatives to China. However, raw cotton or yarn production does not by itself amount to an ammunition supply capability.
Linters must be separated, purified and converted into military-grade nitrocellulose at specialized chemical plants that operate under strict safety and quality requirements. No plans to export output from MKE’s new facility have been announced.

African state joins Trump deportation drive

African state joins Trump deportation drive
Liberia has agreed to accept up to 1,200 third-country migrants deported from the US under a controversial agreement pushed by the Trump administration as part of its sweeping immigration crackdown.
The transfers will take place over one year, with the first group of 20 due to arrive in the West African country on Thursday, Liberia’s Ministry of Information said in a statement on Tuesday.
The arrangement, concluded through an exchange of diplomatic notes in September 2025, covers medically cleared nationals of “African and Western Hemisphere countries.” Those transferred may apply for asylum in Liberia or leave the country voluntarily, the ministry stated.
It said the deportees “are not criminals” and will be treated as guests rather than prisoners. The government said it would provide protection and support during their stay.
Monrovia insisted that the arrangement “is not a transaction with a quid pro quo” and that Liberia “has not demanded or received any compensation or promise of reward.” However, it said the country “will receive support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly,” without disclosing the value or terms of the assistance.
The deal is among the largest reached under US President Donald Trump’s expanding third-country deportation policy. The mechanism allows Washington to remove migrants to states where they hold no citizenship or established ties, including when their home governments refuse to receive them.
A coalition of rights lawyers and advocates, including the Global Strategic Litigation Council, has accused Washington of using third-country transfers to bypass protection orders and expose migrants to persecution or torture. Thousands have reportedly been transferred to nearly two dozen states, including around ten in Africa.
Ghana, Eswatini, Rwanda, Uganda, South Sudan, Equatorial Guinea, and the Central African Republic are among the African countries that have accepted third-country deportees.
The arrangements have triggered legal challenges across the continent. In June, rights lawyers sued Ghana at the Economic Community of West African States Community Court of Justice, accusing Accra of facilitating the onward removal of protected migrants to states where they faced abuse.
A US Senate Foreign Relations Committee minority report said Washington had sent more than $32 million to foreign governments in direct connection with third-country deportation deals by the end of January.
Liberia has said its participation is “entirely humanitarian,” pointing to its founding as a refuge for freed slaves from the US and elsewhere, as well as its history of sheltering people fleeing persecution and war.

The move comes as the use of generative AI among young people has expanded, while researchers, parents and policymakers have raised concerns about children's exposure to inappropriate material, reliance on chatbots for emotional support and the effects of AI on learning.
OpenAI has also faced legal scrutiny over teenagers' use of ChatGPT, including lawsuits from families alleging the chatbot contributed to their children's suicides, increasing pressure on the company to strengthen protections for minors.

The figure was the lowest quarterly rate since 2005.
Türkiye’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declined by 0.3 percentage points from the previous quarter to 7.9 percent in the April-June period, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Aug. 19.
The figure was the lowest quarterly rate in the data series dating back to 2005.
The number of unemployed people aged 15 and over fell by 84,000 to 2.8 million. The unemployment rate was 6.7 percent among men and 10.3 percent among women.
Employment increased by 155,000 to 32.48 million, lifting the employment rate by 0.1 percentage points to 48.5 percent. The rate stood at 65.8 percent for men and 31.6 percent for women.
The labor force expanded by 71,000 to 35.28 million, while the participation rate edged down by 0.1 points to 52.7 percent.
Youth unemployment, covering those aged 15 to 24, fell by 1 percentage point to 13.9 percent. The rate was 11 percent among young men and 19.3 percent among young women.
The composite labor underutilization rate, which also includes time-related underemployment and the potential labor force, declined by 0.2 percentage points to 29.9 percent.

Sumit Sarkar: The Citizen Historian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:14:48 UTC
21:14:48 KST

Professor Sumit Sarkar significantly impacted the understanding of Indian nationalism, illuminating its intricacies through comprehensive analysis. He explored the evolution of nationalism, internal disputes, and collective movements, while challenging conventional binaries. His focus on ordinary people's cravings for justice defined his contributions as a public thinker and citizen historian. This article pays tribute to his influential teaching and the lasting academic heritage he leaves behind.
Professor Sumit Sarkar, widely regarded as among the finest historians of modern Indian history, was educated at Presidency College and the University of Calcutta, and went on to teach for 30 years in the Department of History, University of Delhi. While his scholarship ranged and roamed over the vast canvas of modern Indian history, some indication of the originality of his vision and the painstaking rigour of his scholarship might be gathered by examining one particular facet. There was a recursive quality to the way he returned to the question of nationalism in colonial India, its critique as much as its self-critique. One sees this in his early essays on the 19th-century Bengali intelligentsia, the path-breaking study of the Swadeshi movement in Bengal, as well as the singularly important essays on Gandhian nationalism.Sarkar was a Marxist historian and, it might surprise some that his scholarship was aimed at democratising the scope of nationalism, in terms of method as much as archive. Nationalism could only be understood in terms of popular aspirations and struggles for justice, be they about land, labour, dignity or representation. In the words of Sarkar, "what was remarkable [about the national movement] was the capacity for internal debate, change and auto-critique…combined with a persistent concern for mass poverty…and the need for mass mobilization [leading] to a progressive broadening of the meanings of freedom.
One need only note that none of the four features central to the [Indian] constitution…democracy based on universal suffrage, secularism, elements of federalism and social justice through affirmative action had been present in the early programs of mainstream nationalism".His study of the Swadeshi movement in Bengal captured this complexity by analysing its radical agenda of complete independence, the rapid connections made between individuals and organisations nationally and internationally, the granular contestations over ideology, and the challenges of mass mobilisation. While Hindu religious symbols and imagery were employed by some for mobilisation, Sarkar shows us that even at the time of the Swadeshi movement, there was a recognition that such invocations of Hindu identity could be read in ways that reinforced narratives of Muslim tyranny or caste privilege.Sarkar documents the efforts made at the time to combat this possibility and to discover cult figures that would appeal to both communities, so as to broaden the scope of the national, with the revolutionary journal Yugantar suggesting a festival to honour Mir Kasim, not unlike those around Shivaji. Sarkar also discusses tensions within the revolutionary movement, including Hemchandra Kanungo's writings of the late 1920s, which critiqued the invocation of Hindu religious imagery as much as arguments of a Hindu golden past in the Swadeshi movement, since this was bound to exclude Muslims, valorise caste privilege, and encourage a cultic devotion to a leader rather than broaden into a mass movement with a political and socio-economic agenda.Kanungo could not be ignored: he was a legend even among revolutionaries, had travelled to Europe to study the technology of the bomb and meet revolutionaries, was imprisoned in the Cellular Jail following his involvement in the Alipore bomb case, and was deeply admired among fellow revolutionaries.While the Swadeshi movement was no doubt central to the formation of nationalism, it had its limitations in terms of its treatment of the communal and caste question, as well as its inability to adequately formulate a broader agrarian programme; these challenges continued well into the period of Gandhian nationalism.This complex and evolving understanding of the phenomenon of nationalism informs Sarkar's critique of theorisations which treat nationalism as captive to the rigid binary between India and the "West". Such theorisations of Indian nationalism, which value it merely in terms of its perceived indigeneity and difference from the "West", fail to recognise the evolving and transformative interaction between the two. Could one question Ambedkar for invoking the French Revolution in the Mahad Satyagraha, or forget Bhagat Singh's invocation of Lenin during his trial?The agenda of nationalism was broadened because of popular movements and local struggles by marginalised sections, so-called lower castes, "tribal" groups, Socialists and Communists. It is this historical and democratic expansion, based on ideals of justice and equality, that characterised the national movement and that, in Sarkar's analysis, distinguished it from Hindutva nationalism. He argued that important strands of the latter retained features visible in its early 20th-century formulations and remained open to critiques made at the time; he also questioned the extent to which questions of mass poverty or socio-economic change occupied a central place within it.Fiercely independent, Sarkar's Marxism did not prevent him from publicly critiquing in the strongest terms the Left government's policies and the events surrounding Singur and Nandigram.Sarkar, therefore, never shied away from drawing on his scholarship to speak as a citizen historian on what he perceived to be the crises of the day wracking the body politic. He was able to occupy that rare position of a public intellectual because his research attended to the fundamental questions that had a direct bearing on the dizzying churns of the present, soaring above the drive for narrow specialisation that can sometimes leave historians unprepared when it comes to addressing the most urgent challenges of the times.Writing this obituary, it is impossible not to remember his small office in which about six of us, privileged students of the MA, sat in 1999-2000 to learn, not Indian history, but the Renaissance and the Reformation in Europe.Professor Sarkar had his lectures meticulously prepared, written in his flowing, slanting hand on foolscap sheets of paper. The lectures lucidly brought alive the worlds of the Renaissance and the Reformation, and moved from Michelangelo's search for the perfect blue and the ambivalence and originality of Machiavelli's 'ethics' to the intricacies of theological dispute, showing how deeply knowledgeable Sarkar was about various aspects of European history.
Amidst the gravity of the issues being discussed, on more than one occasion there was the unmistakable, almost child-like mischievous humour that would surface, his face breaking into a smile, the tone and voice assuming the sharp edge of an irreverence that is perhaps always inseparable from great learning.It was very painful meeting Professor Sarkar in the years of his illness, which he bore with remarkable and rare fortitude. Farewell Professor Sarkar, even as you remain in the gift of your teaching and in the luminosity of your works.Rahul Govind was a student of Sumit Sarkar at the University of Delhi. He has a PhD. from Columbia University and is currently Professor of History at the University of Delhi.

Putin’s Mach-10 wonder weapon misses by 30 meters. Russia stopped building it in April.
Unknown

2026-08-19
12:14:01 UTC
21:14:01 KST

- As more Russian missiles rain down on Ukrainian cities, one munition is curiously absent
- The Mach-10 Kinzhal, an air-launched ballistic missile, has been missing in action for months now
- Ukrainian intelligence says the Kremlin halted production in April because the missile kept missing by 30 meters
Russia's Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missile, a version of the ground-launched Iskander, travels as far as 2,000 km at 10 times the speed of sound while packing a 500-kg warhead. It was one of a clutch of purported super-weapons that Russian Pres. Vladimir Putin revealed in a dramatic announcement in 2018.
Launched in mid-air by specially modified Mikoyan MiG-31 interceptors in order to boost its speed and range, the Kinzhal is, in theory, a powerful deep strike munition capable of blasting right through all but the best and rarest air defenses.
In practice, it kept missing. Russia stopped building the $4.5-million missile in April, Maj. Gen. Vadym Skibitskyi, Ukraine's deputy chief of defense intelligence, told RBC-Ukraine—and the rocket fuel and components that had gone into Kinzhals now go into Iskanders, sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles, and air-launched Kh-101 cruise missiles instead.
The reason is a number. A missile of this class needs to land within five to seven meters of its aim point to be worth firing. The Kinzhal, according to Skibitskyi, lands within 30 meters or more. "We can hardly recall a single instance where this missile hit the target precisely," he said. Satellite imagery of the Ukrainian air base at Starokostiantyniv, a favorite Kinzhal target, shows the craters ringing the airfield rather than sitting on it.
The Kolomna Machine Building Design Bureau reportedly produced 44 Kinzhals in 2024 and 144 in 2025. The line climbed for two years and then stopped dead.
The Kinzhal isn't the only munition reportedly getting the ax. The Kremlin is also halting production of the Kh-32 air-launched cruise missile, which Russian engineers repeatedly failed to improve before the program was sent back for further work. "This would explain why Russia has not launched any Kinzhals for multiple months, and very few Kh-32s," AMK Mapping noted.
At least one analyst anticipated this development years ago. Way back in 2022, Carnegie Endowment analyst Michael Kofman wrote that he didn't "understand the interest in Russian use of Kinzhal. There's nothing special or particularly exciting about this system." It is, according to Kofman, just an Iskander but with a more complicated and expensive launch method.
It may have taken the Russians a few years to come to the same conclusion. The last Kinzhal strike might have been on 14 May, when the Russians launched three Kinzhals as part of a wider strike on Ukrainian cities involving 731 missiles and drones.
The purported Kinzhal shutdown, if true, could orphan the boutique fleet of around two dozen MiG-31K/I interceptors whose main role is to haul a Kinzhal to high altitude before launch. The Kinzhal carriers account for around 20% of the wider MiG-31 fleet, whose main mission is air defense over the vast Russian interior.
The MiGs may end up as victims of ruthless efficiency-seeking. If Skibitskyi is right, the Kremlin simply can't afford to keep every munition in production as it seeks to escalate its bombardment of Ukrainian cities amid growing economic losses from Ukrainian deep strikes targeting Russian strategic industries.
It's possible the only way the Russians can boost production of their best deep strike munitions is to cut production of the underperforming ones. According to the pro-Ukrainian Conflict Intelligence Team, the savings in fuel, components, and funds from the suspended Kinzhal and Kh-32 assembly lines "were redirected to other types of missiles."
Production winners and losers
Trending Now
That's how, in July, Russia reportedly produced 65 Iskanders, surpassing its target of 60 by nearly 10%. Meanwhile, production of Kh-101s reached 140% of the monthly target. Kalibr production 111%. Across its main missile lines, Russian industry is running at 110 to 120% of plan. Certain Russian munitions may soon disappear from the sky over Ukraine, if they haven't already. But only because more copies of better munitions are taking their place.
Ironically, the Kinzhals and their carriers are fading away at the same time Ukraine's own deep strike forces may have landed their most powerful blow against the aerial hypersonic strike force. On 15 August, a barrage of Ukrainian drones and cruise missiles struck a range of targets deep inside Russia.
Among the targets was Savasleyka air base, in Nizhny Novgorod around 785 km from Ukraine. "Direct hits and fires reported," WarTranslated noted.
Among other aircraft, Savasleyka air base hosts some of the MiG-31Ks that carry Kinzhal missiles. Or once carried them, if Skibitskyi is correct and the missile has fallen out of use. It's unclear whether the attack on Savasleyka damaged or destroyed any MiG-31s.
Even if the Kinzhal launchers burned to the ground, it may be too late to matter. The Russians may have rendered the planes and their missiles irrelevant before the Ukrainians could drone them.

FSSAI action prompts Amway, Emami, four other brands to drop '100%' product claims

FSSAI action prompts Amway, Emami, four other brands to drop '100%' product claims
Edited by: Rajeev Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 19, 2026, 17:42 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
FSSAI has recently taken action against companies operating in several segments.
NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has stepped up action against food companies using "100%" claims on product labels and in advertisements, saying several firms have now removed such claims following regulatory intervention.The food regulator said on Wednesday that six food business operators had taken corrective steps after being asked to discontinue the use of "100%" on labels, packaging, promotional material and advertisements.Among the companies that changed their labelling were Amway India, Emami, Bonn Biscuits, Apis India, Juza Foods and Masterchow Foods.FSSAI said Bonn Biscuits had used a "100%" claim in an advertisement for its Bonn Cummin Flavor Jeera Bite Biscuits, 76 gm. The company has since removed the claim from its website.Emami was also asked to address its use of a 100 per cent claim for Zhandu Honey. According to FSSAI, the company complied with its advisory and took corrective action.Apis India has removed similar claims from its honey products, the regulator said.Amway India Enterprises had been using the claim "100% Pure Coconut Oil" for one of its products. Following FSSAI's intervention, the company submitted a compliance response confirming that it had voluntarily removed "100%" from its packaging and promotional material.
The company also told the regulator that older stock carrying the claim had been discontinued from sales channels.Kerala-based Juza Foods has removed 100 per cent claims from several of its baby food products, while Masterchow Foods has taken down a similar claim from its Ramen Noodle product.
The action is part of a wider FSSAI drive against what it considers misleading claims in food labelling and advertising. The regulator has been asking food business operators to stop using the term "100%" where it could create a misleading impression about a product.FSSAI has also taken enforcement action against several other food businesses in recent months, including companies in the energy drink and alcoholic beverage sectors.The regulator said on Tuesday that six companies, including Dabur India and Ferns N Petals, had corrected issues identified in notices concerning misleading labels, claims and advertisements.Earlier on Sunday, FSSAI said another six food companies had taken corrective measures, including withdrawing misleading labels and trademarks, after receiving notices for alleged violations of food safety laws.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

Rai pulling plug on Ranucci 'would be political decision'
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
14:11:20 CEST
21:11:20 KST

Any decision by state broadcaster Rai
to possibly suspend or replace Sigfrido Ranucci would be
political and tainted by falsehoods about the investigative
journalist whose home was bombed by a controversial friend and
former Berlusconi pimping and graft associate in October,
Ranucci's lawyer said Wednesday.
                                    
                                       
				The friend, Valter Lavitola, has said he regrets the trouble he
caused Ranucci by staging the bomb attack, allegedly to help get
the journalist's security escort boosted, calling Ranucci a
"brother".
                                    
                                       
				Businessman, ex journalist and restaurateur Lavitola has
admitted organising the attack but claimed he only wanted the
gang allegedly coordinated by his Cameroonian go-between to let
off a few rounds at the residence at Pomezia south of Rome, and
not plant a bomb that destroyed Ranucci's and his daughter's
cars and might have killed her.
                                    
                                       
				Government members, led by right-wing League leader, Deputy
Premier and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini, have called for
Ranucci to be suspended by Rai over his
allegedly murky relationship with Lavitola.
                                    
                                       
				Right-wing politicians have also slammed the reporter for
comparing himself to late Italian civic heroes and terror and
Cosa Nostra martyrs like Aldo Moro, Piersanti Mattarella,
Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino in a post last week in
which he said Italy killed "all its best" in order to stop and
silence them.
                                    
                                       
				Critics have also said Ranucci has failed to criticise Lavitola
for the attack.
                                    
                                       
				Premier Giorgia Meloni's right-wing Brothers of Italy (FdI) has
also called on centre-left opposition Democratic Party (PD)
leader Elly Schlein to apologise for alleg edly suggesting the
government might have been linked to the attack, immediately
after it happened.
                                    
                                       
				Ranucci presents Report, an exposè programme that has frequently
irked politicians, mostly on the right of the political
spectrum, and which has been often sued by them without much
success.
                                    
                                       
				Ranucci's lawyer Roberto De Vita said Wednesday: "Any initiative
Rai were to take at this time regarding Sigfrido Ranucci, and
therefore the Report program, would inevitably be tainted by
falsehoods that, despite the clear and unequivocal position of
the judicial authorities regarding the victim and his
unawareness, have been incessantly fueled by specious
controversies, even within the company."
De Vita said that Rai was considering pulling the plug on his
client for "incompatibility" and added:
"Any further justification would be subject to the already
expressed conditioning indications of government and
institutional leaders, placing Rai's initiatives towards the
host and the programme within the sphere of political
decision-making."
Right-wing politicians and commentators have suggested Ranucci
knew about the attack, a claim prosecutors have not echoed.
                                    
                                       
				The prosecutors have said the attack was meant by Lavitola to
boost his friend's standing in view of a possible entry into
politics, from which Lavitola also hoped to benefit.
                                    
                                       
				Lavitola has denied this.
                                    
                                       
				Lavitola has been at the centre of many top political and
business corruption stories over the years.
                                    
                                       
				These include: a Monte Carlo house whose purchase sank former
Silvio Berlusconi protegé Gianfranco Fini's political career;
the alleged buying and selling of Senators by Berlusconi to try
to bring down a centre-left government led by ex European
Commission president Romano Prodi; the attempted extortion of 
Berlusconi
over a ring of escorts at his 'elegant dinners'; kickbacks for
contracts in Panama; and scams involving publishing funds.
                                    
                                       
				Ranucci said Tuesday night that it was up to Rai to suspend or
replace him. He also said it was not up to parliamentary
anti-mafia commission chair Chiara Colosimo, a member of
Meloni's FdI party, to decide on the size of his escort after
she said it should be cut.
                                    
                                       
				Ranucci already had a two-strong escort before the attack, and
afterwards it was boosted to six.
                                    
                                       
				Conservative daily Libero reported Wednesday that the state
broadcaster had decided to suspend the journalist pending the
result of the investigation into the bombing.
                                    
                                       
				Also on Wednesday, Ranucci said he was suing Rome appeals court
magistrate Clementina Forleo over a post on Sunday in which she
said: "Who is blackmailing Ranucci? Why does he want to stay at
the helm of Report (a public service broadcast) at all costs by
threatening to expose chats with "everyone"? And who are the
"everyone" he's talking about?"
Forleo responded by saying she was only commenting on news that
had been published in the media and not denied.
                                    
                                       
				Ranucci's predecessor as long-time host of Report, Milena
Gabanelli, said Wednesday she had no interest in returning to
her former post.
                                    
                                       
				Gabanelli, like several other former Rai journalists, has since
moved to left-leaning TV broadcaster L7.
                                    
                                       
				The Italian opposition has claimed Meloni has taken over Rai,
calling it 'TeleMeloni'.
                                    
                                       
				Report's left-leaning stance stands in marked contrast to this
claim.
                                    
                                       
				
photo: Ranucci (L) and Lavitola

Water conflict around the German capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:10:00 UTC
21:10:00 KST

Amid extreme heat, water grows scarce around Berlin
August 19, 2026
For years, Petra Liesenfeld has witnessed falling groundwater levels in her hometown of Baruth. She has to water her garden far more often than she used to, and has seen some local trees completely dry out. At the same time, two beverage companies are looking to expand production in the area.
Mineral water has been bottled in the small town of Baruth, which lies around 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin, since the 1990s. The site is now run by Red Bull and Austrian beverage producer Rauch, who are planning a new canning factory and additional facilities. All in the middle of a water protection area.
The Baruth waterworks are licensed to extract a fixed amount of groundwater each year, just 8% of which goes to supply the town's roughly 4,300 residents with drinking water. The remaining 92% is reserved for Red Bull and Rauch, and is enough to cover the drinking water needs of 57,000 people. But exactly how much water the companies currently use is not made public.
This is legal under the existing contracts, said Peter Ilk, who until recently was the town's mayor and is considered a driving force behind the region's industrialization. He sees no problem with the way water is managed.
"We have always given priority to supplying the population. That is also written into all the contracts," he said, adding that it stands to reason that the companies need more than the town's residents. "That's how you end up with this ratio of around one to 10 in terms of consumption."
Old data informing current decisions
Hydrogeologist Irina Engelhardt from the Technical University in Berlin takes a more critical view, pointing out that the contracts, which are around 30 years old, are based on outdated information. Since then, groundwater levels, groundwater recharge and the way land is used have all changed significantly.
"I am concerned at how the water situation is developing in the state of Brandenburg," she said. "The volume that is actually available is currently being overestimated by the Brandenburg authorities."
Together with a citizens' initiative made up of local residents, she is calling for new, independent assessments — and for clear and open communication. Though the authorities granted them access to some groundwater monitoring documents, large parts were redacted, which some residents believe is a move to conceal information about changes in levels.
"We ask ourselves why there can't be more transparency if everything is aboveboard. Why isn't the public allowed to know?" said Petra Liesenfeld.
Exactly how much Red Bull and Rauch pay for their daily extraction of up to 7 million liters of groundwater is not public information.
DW approached both companies for comment, but by the time of publication, neither had responded.
For drought researcher Andreas Marx, this lack of transparency is problematic.
"By law, water is a public commodity. It cannot be privately owned. So, in my view, every decision made and every contract signed over its use should be open to the public," he said.
How dry is Brandenburg?
Germany — and Brandenburg — are still water-rich regions. Marx, who heads the Drought Monitor at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, said "the challenge isn't adapting to permanent water scarcity but learning how to cope with dry periods that can last two or even three years."
Nevertheless, the water balance in the state, as elsewhere in Germany, is definitely changing. Since the 2018 drought, groundwater has not been sufficiently replenished in many places and higher temperatures and increasing evaporation are making it harder for reserves in deeper soil layers to recover.
This could cause even more problems in the future, as 95% of Brandenburg's drinking water comes from groundwater.
How much water does the energy transition need?
In Grünheide, in the eastern part of the state of Brandenburg, Tesla's Gigafactory has a permit to extract up to 1.4 million cubic meters of water per year and is planning to expand production to as many as 7,500 vehicles per week. Meanwhile, in recent years, residents have repeatedly been urged to save water.
"Many projects, including new schools and kindergartens, were put on hold because there simply wasn't enough water," said local resident Manu Hoyer.
Marx said when water resources are scarce, residents are generally the first to face restrictions because they're the easiest to limit. "Industrial companies are rarely restricted, because the economic consequences are much harder to assess," he said.
Copper for the energy transition — a risk to groundwater?
The potential for an additional water problem is brewing further south in Spremberg, where a large mine is planned. Over the coming decades, copper — which is essential for power grids, electric vehicles and the transition to clean energy — is set to be extracted from depths of up to 1,200 meters (about 4,000 feet).
Geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeifer said mine water from such depths is highly saline and sulfurous and requires extensive treatment.
"But the treatment plant proposed so far is nowhere near capable of doing what's actually required to clean the water to a standard where it could be safely discharged into the Spree," Pfeiffer said of the river that flows north toward Berlin.
The river water is already affected by decades of lignite mining in the region, and it is facing additional pressures. With lignite extraction set to end by 2038, the groundwater currently pumped into the Spree from the mines will no longer be available. As a result, dry summers could see the river carrying up to 75% less water, with far-reaching consequences for water resources all the way to Berlin.
Could rainfall be stored for future use?
One possible solution to the water problems facing the state around the German capital is artificial groundwater recharge, where excess water from periods of high rainfall is stored underground and used later.
Hydrogeologist Engelhardt is researching where this could be possible in the region.
"There are areas in Brandenburg — such as where Tesla is now located — where artificial groundwater recharge could meet almost the entire demand of the local drinking water supplier," she said.
However, enough available water is necessary for this solution to work.
For drought researcher Marx, one question remains crucial: What rules should determine how water is distributed between the population, agriculture, nature and industry during prolonged dry periods?
As the global temperature continues to rise, it's not just an issue reserved for Brandenburg — or even Germany.
This article was originally written in German.
Correction, August 19, 2026: An earlier version of this article misspelled the name of geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeifer. DW apologizes for the error.

Iran executed at least 900 people since January, rights group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:08:23 UTC
21:08:23 KST

The Abdorrahman Boroumand Center documented 901 executions in the first seven months of 2026, including 56 on political or national security charges and 98 members of ethnic minorities — a further rise in death penalties in the Islamic Republic in recent years.
Iran has executed at least 900 people since the beginning of 2026, including 28 executions carried out in August alone, according to a report released by the Washington-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran.
The rights group documented 901 executions between January and July, highlighting what it described as a sharp increase in the use of capital punishment across cases involving national security, drug-related offences and members of ethnic minorities.
At least 56 people were executed during the seven-month period on political or national security charges, including 29 people linked to public protests, 13 accused of espionage and 14 sentenced on other security-related charges. Drug-related offences accounted for at least 268 executions.
The figures also show a disproportionate impact on ethnic minorities and other vulnerable groups.
Between January and July, at least 98 members of ethnic minorities were executed, including 40 Baluch people, 29 Kurds, 21 Afghans, six Arabs, one Turk and one Turkman.
The report also documented the executions of 16 women and two people who were under the age of 18 at the time of their alleged offences. Five executions were carried out publicly.
Executions were concentrated in several provinces, with Razavi Khorasan recording the highest number at 95, followed by Isfahan with 71 and Alborz with 57.
The latest figures add to growing international concern over the scale of executions in Iran.
In a report to the United Nations General Assembly, Secretary-General António Guterres said at least 975 people were reportedly executed in Iran in 2024, a 17% increase from the previous year and the highest annual figure recorded since 2015.
The report also documented a further sharp rise in the first half of 2025, with at least 612 executions recorded between January and June, or 119% more compared with the same period in 2024.
The UN has repeatedly raised concerns over the use of the death penalty in Iran, particularly in cases involving drug offences, national security charges and ethnic minorities, as well as over fair-trial guarantees and the use of torture-tainted confessions.

South Africa citrus exporters secure breakthrough in India

21:07:33 KST

South Africa citrus exporters secure breakthrough in India
South African citrus exporters have received a boost in the Indian market after New Delhi amended its plant quarantine rules on Monday, approving additional cold-treatment options for fresh citrus imports from the African state.
The move, which follows almost a decade of negotiations, will give exporters more flexibility and could help improve the quality of fruit reaching the Indian market. Minister of Agriculture Willie Aucamp welcomed the development, saying it was good news for the industry and showed how technology was helping farmers overcome barriers and expand access to international markets.
He said it would help South African farmers push the boundaries and enable other countries to benefit from the country’s high-quality agricultural produce. “This is not only good news, but also indicates how advanced technology enable our farmers to push barriers to have other countries enjoy our high-quality produce,” Aucamp noted.
India is home to about 1.47 billion people and is one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing economies, making it a potentially important market for South African citrus.
CEO of the Citrus Growers’ Association of Southern Africa (CGA), Boitshoko Ntshabele, argued the focus should now shift to improving the commercial conditions for South African citrus exports to India. He said tariffs of about 25% to 30% continue to put South African citrus at a disadvantage compared with competitors from the Southern Hemisphere that have preferential trade arrangements with India.
“Special recognition is given to the Department of Agriculture and Citrus Research International for their continued technical engagement with Indian authorities that have made the new treatment options possible. This demonstrates the importance of sustained public-private partnership in improving technical conditions for accessing markets,” Ntshabele said.
“We look forward to working with the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition on the critical task of addressing these tariff barriers and improving the competitiveness of South African citrus in the Indian market going forward.”

U.S. Navy invests $50M in Shield AI’s runway-free strike drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:07:28 UTC
21:07:28 KST

- The U.S. Navy, PAE Aviation and the Defense Innovation Unit are investing $50 million to scale runway-independent maritime strike drones built around Shield AI's X-BAT.
- The RIMES program aims to give Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, which lack the flight decks for fixed-wing aircraft, a strike capability that can launch and land vertically.
The U.S. Navy’s Rapid Capability Office, PAE Aviation and the Defense Innovation Unit are investing $50 million to scale unmanned, runway-independent maritime strike capabilities built around Shield AI’s X-BAT aircraft, the Navy announced.
The funding falls under the Runway Independent Maritime Expeditionary Strike program, or RIMES, which the Defense Innovation Unit and Navy launched in February to develop a strike drone capable of operating from surface combatants that lack the flight decks, catapults or arrested landing systems conventional carrier-based aircraft require. The Navy’s Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, with 74 hulls currently active in the fleet, can land a helicopter but cannot deploy a fixed-wing strike aircraft, a gap the program is intended to close.
The investment builds on existing risk-reduction work led by the PAE Aviation Rapid Capability Cell with Shield AI. The award was made using the Middle Tier of Acquisition Rapid Prototype approach and an Other Transaction Authority contract, according to the Navy.
X-BAT is a vertical takeoff and landing, jet-powered aircraft Shield AI first unveiled in October 2025. The company has said the aircraft has a range exceeding 2,000 nautical miles (3,700 kilometers) with a full mission payload, a service ceiling above 50,000 feet (15,240 meters), and a wingspan of about 39 feet (11.9 meters). Shield AI has said X-BAT is designed for strike, counter-air, electronic warfare and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions, and that its Hivemind autonomy software allows it to operate in communications-denied or degraded environments.
“Airpower without runways is the holy grail of deterrence,” Shield AI co-founder and president Brandon Tseng said when the aircraft was unveiled. “It gives our forces persistence, reach and survivability, and it buys diplomacy another day.”
Shield AI has said X-BAT will initially be powered by GE Aerospace’s F110-GE-129 engine, with a first flight targeted for 2026. The company already supplies the Navy and other services with its smaller V-BAT unmanned aircraft, which has flown more than 170 sorties in Ukraine and supports a nearly $200 million Coast Guard contract for contractor-owned intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance services.
The $50 million RIMES investment does not disclose a timeline for X-BAT flight testing or deployment aboard Navy destroyers, and the Navy has not said how many aircraft the program is expected to procure.

Ukraine Spots AI-Generated Russian Advance Video—Giant Soldiers and Even the Buildings Are Fake

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Spots AI-Generated Russian Advance Video—Giant Soldiers and Even the Buildings Are Fake
Russian forces are turning to AI-generated battlefield footage to manufacture evidence of advances they cannot convincingly demonstrate on the ground, according to Ukrainian OSINT group DeepState on August 18.
DeepState said Russian sources recently published a video that was presented as proof that Russian troops had infiltrated the outskirts of Oskil.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The footage, however, appears to have been generated with artificial intelligence rather than recorded at the location, according to the group’s analysis.
DeepState pointed to several visual anomalies in the video. Entire buildings appear to have been generated, while structures that should be hangars were transformed into private homes in parts of the footage.
Russian troops depicted in the clip also show distorted proportions and other visual artifacts characteristic of AI-generated imagery.
The episode appears to represent a digital evolution of Russia’s so-called “flag-planting” tactic, in which small groups are sent forward to raise a Russian flag at a location and film it as supposed evidence of territorial control, even when Russian forces do not actually hold the area.
DeepState described the emerging practice as “AI flag planting,” suggesting Russian commanders may increasingly use generative tools to create the appearance of battlefield gains without having to send troops forward to produce the footage physically.
According to the Ukrainian OSINT group, the apparent shift may reflect the growing risks associated with traditional flag-planting missions, where troops can be exposed and killed simply to create propaganda footage claiming an advance.
Usually, Russian forces send actual troops instead of generating them with AI to create propaganda videos.
Recently, Ukrainian troops captured a Russian soldier who appeared in a propaganda video presenting the Ukrainian-controlled village of Zirnytsia in the Zaporizhzhia region as having been seized by Russian forces.
Ukraine’s 142nd Separate Mechanized Brigade said the prisoner was a serviceman of Russia’s 5th Tank Brigade who had been sent to the area to display a Russian flag and record footage that could later be presented as evidence of a Russian advance.

'Something smells off': The Netanyahu backer behind two propaganda initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:06:10 UTC
21:06:10 KST

The name Avi Gross may not be the most immediately recognizable name among Benjamin Netanyahu's supporters. Yet he is the businessman behind at least two propaganda initiatives to disseminate the Likud's messages during election campaigns, a Haaretz investigation reveals.
Gross, who had been invited as a guest of honor to a Netanyahu speech before the U.S. Congress in 2024, is the man behind the content production company New Vision Production, located in Petah Tikva, central Israel. Establishing the studios with their advanced equipment had cost millions of shekels, sources confirmed to Haaretz. Gross himself declined to respond to Haaretz's inquiries.
Founded about a year ago, NVP operates along two separate but tangential tracks. One is to provide paid content services for the Likud campaign (which the party confirmed, stating that it was done legally). The second, as revealed by Haaretz, is the distribution of viral videos taken from podcasts that the company produces for Netanyahu-supporting media personalities. The Likud stated that the party has no connection to these podcasts, which leaves the question: who actually funds them?
There is also another track, perhaps only semi-official, where the company's premises serve as a kind of production house for ostensibly private videos that align with the campaign's messages (the party denies any connection). An analysis of these reveals that at least seven "content creators" filmed independent videos that, whether by chance or not, promoted the Likud campaign's messages and attacked Netanyahu's rivals and the media.
Some of the videos were produced even before the party contracted with the company. The list of creators includes, among others, Channel 14 reporter Tamir Schneid, panelist Noam Fathi, Likud spokesman Guy Levy, and Adi Shamai Hacohen – who was behind the "coming out" video "Mom, Dad, I'm a Bibist."
Since these are ostensibly private creators, "they are not subject to legal restrictions," a legal source involved in election law told Haaretz. But when everything is done in a single complex, the dots almost connect themselves: Welcome to the propaganda studios.
The current project is not the first time Gross has acted on Netanyahu's behalf in an election campaign. In 2021, he established Lychee Productions, which was behind "The Trial," a propaganda film distributed about a week before the November 2022 election that cast aspersions on the law enforcement system, "Case 4000" against Netanyahu, and the media. Over the years, Gross also published numerous posts on his social media accounts expressing support for Netanyahu and echoing his government's messages.
Gross, a 66-year-old resident of Mikhmoret, made his fortune in textiles, got into technology companies as a partner and founded the Panda mattresses company which he recently sold to Hollandia, in which he now holds 9 percent. He had been linked to the possible acquisition of the Maccabi Netanya soccer team but no deal ensued.
Gross is not officially connected to NVP. According to the Registrar of Companies, it was founded in July 2025 as "Neve Hadar Productions" by Neve Pinchas (who is defined as the company's CEO and, sources say, is responsible for content production). Until recently, the company had not been publicly credited with any product.
But this May, things moved quickly: its name was changed to NVP, it moved to Petah Tikva, it got a website and a month later, 90 percent of its shares were transferred to an American company whose owners' identity is unknown. The company, Great Production 2026 LLC, was incorporated in April in Delaware, which does not require shareholders to be divulged.
Although Gross does not appear in the company's documents at all, two sources well-versed in the details confirmed to Haaretz that he is the businessman behind the establishment of the media initiative in Petah Tikva.
Service vendors
Possibly, the word "initiative" does not adequately reflect the project's scale and scope of influence, especially how little the time it has been operating. In just five weeks, the company published dozens of short videos with pro-Netanyahu content, some of which garnered thousands of likes and tens of thousands of views. The sources of the videos are four new podcasts with at least 15 episodes.
The hosts include Netanyahu's brother Ido Netanyahu as well as personalities associated with media outlets such as Channel 14 and Galey Israel Radio, including Efi Mordechai – who brought us the "Ulpanometer," a venture to measure leftist presence on screen.
It doesn't end there. NVP also began providing services to Gadi Taub and his podcast group "Gatekeeper," featuring among others Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz. A new podcast called "The Nationalists," hosted by Alon Malik and Bat-El Benyamin, was recently added to the gallery of locally produced podcasts.
However, the studio recordings, all edited professionally, also include less regulated initiatives, where the only thing that seems orderly is the messages: a suspicious resemblance to the Likud campaign, and primarily – an attack on the mainstream media. For example, Channel 14 personality Noam Fathi filmed a propaganda video in the podcast studio against Channel 12 News (following a libel suit filed against him by the channel and Guy Peleg over his remarks regarding the Sde Teiman affair).
"Active Info" investigators, in collaboration with Haaretz, managed to verify by by means of geolocation and image comparison that additional propaganda videos were filmed in the Petah Tikva studio complex in recent months. For example, two government-supporting content creators, Yishai Gvirtzman and Dana Cohen, popularly dubbed "Dana Banana," filmed a video attacking the media from the complex's inner courtyard, which is only accessible after a security check and by invitation from someone working there.
Two other people who appear on the list of creators working there are spokesman Guy Levy and Tamir Schneid, Channel 14's "special affairs" reporter (going by the footage, it appears that at least one of the affairs is a clash over Case 4000). Both filmed in and outside the studios. At least in Levy's case, who echoed a message that Gadi Eisenkot – Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming election – sought to end the war, the timing is key. He did so before July 27 but also after that date, and in the 90 days preceding the elections, election laws become critical.
The advent of NVP also changed the working method of Shamai Hacohen (from the "coming out" video). In June, even before the Likud began working with NVP, he switched his usual filming location from home to the studio in Petah Tikva. From there, for example, he launched an attack against Ronen Tzur, who called for Channel 14 to be shut down, or against media outlets that did not sufficiently sing Netanyahu's praises after the day of battle with Iran about two months ago.
Beyond the unofficial recordings, NVP is also responsible for official video content in the Likud campaign. So far, it has published about 20 videos in that context, mostly against Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, incorporating two messages: "It's them or a broad national government" and "Eisenkot is not Yashar, he's left-wing." NVP is also responsible for the AI video showing Eisenkot running with outstretched arms toward a young man resembling his son who was killed in Gaza, but at the last moment he ignores him and embraces United Arab List chairman Mansour Abbas. The creator of this video is none other than Neve Pinchas, the company's founder, who still holds 10 percent of its shares.
"Something smells off," the legal source cognizant of election law told Haaretz. But asked if it goes beyond stink, he says it's a gray area, very much so. According to him, Israel's election laws are outdated and not suitable for 2026 and the social media era. Additionally, the fact that the videos aren't published by the party itself makes it hard to show connection between it and the distribution process.
Ultimately, he says, it will be a challenge to prove that the law had been broken. All will depend on the interpretation of the Central Elections Committee chairman, Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Solberg, and the evidence presented to him. "Part of the problem with current legislation is that the law doesn't apply to unofficial campaigns," he stresses. Thus they can bypass the law. "This is not the first time this has been done, but in the past, it was much more minor and subtle," he says.
On July 19, the members of the Likud Constitution, Law and Justice Committee received an invitation signed by Minister Haim Katz, to a special meeting to discuss the reserved slots the prime minister wanted on the party's Knesset slate. The location chosen for the gathering was NVP's offices in Petah Tikva. Ultimately the meeting was moved, but this does not mean the complex was erased from the Likud's map; on the contrary. Haaretz learned that in recent weeks, the studios have become a coveted destination for the prime minister himself.
In August alone, Netanyahu was documented there three times: once as a guest on Taub's podcast, a second time to film a video in which he announced a reserved slot for Oren Dobronsky on the Likud slate, and a third time for the strange story of the Army Radio program; last week, the military station published an episode of the podcast "King of Creating Life," featuring the prime minister, and for some reason, it was not filmed at the station's Jaffa base but in the Petah Tikva studios. The station explained that Netanyahu's office told them that the filming had to be moved due to security considerations. A security source told Haaretz that the Dignitary Protection Unit had not made any such demand.
Either way, according to several testimonies, Netanyahu's frequent visits to the studios cause difficulty and inconveniences for employees in the building. They receive no prior notice and before every visit, the Dignitary Protection Unit prevents employees from leaving their offices until filming is complete.
Getting credit
Another name arising in several contexts is attorney Ophir Falk, who became the prime minister's political adviser in 2023. The year before that, he partnered in the creation of Netanyahu's book "My Story," which was part of the election campaign that year and distributed in the week preceding it, and according to a source who spoke with Haaretz, he was paid for it from Sela Meir publishing house. The second – he was a partner in Lychee Productions (and held 30 percent of its shares until it was dissolved), and joined Gross in creating "The Trial." This film, which was promoted exclusively and primarily on the Walla website and social media – and also by Netanyahu himself – reached millions of views; all this just a few days before the elections.
Yinon Magal, host of "The Patriots" on Channel 14, was also involved in the film. His voice is not heard and his face does not appear on screen, but Haaretz learned that he received payment for his participation just six months before he testified for the prosecution in the Netanyahu trial. In fact, Magal, whose name appears in the credits at the end of the film, interviewed most of the participants.
Lychee, owned by Gross and Falk, invested significantly in promoting and distributing the film. It set up social media pages, disseminated video clips and of course marketed the 40-minute film itself. It was also distributed by Netanyahu and his son Yair, as well as among opinion leaders supporting the government, such as Taub, Galit Distel-Atbaryan, spokesman Guy Levy, and Magal himself, even though he did not state that he participated in the project. In early 2025, shortly before it was finally dissolved in March of that year, Lychee released a sequel, "The Trial 2," featuring some of the original film's participants. As often happens, the sequel did not reach the heights of the original film.
In addition to Avi Gross, NVP also declined to comment but last week it stated, "NVP is a leading production company. The company is engaged in producing independent content alongside providing professional production services to diverse clients. As a policy, the company does not discuss its clients' affairs or projects in the media. The company operates in compliance with all laws, and invites entities from across Israel's business, social, and public spectrum to enjoy its professional services."
Other subjects of the article did not provide responses either. Haaretz contacted the content creators filmed at NVP's complex and asked if they paid, received payment, or were connected to the company. Dana Cohen, Yishai Gvirtzman, Adi Shamai Hacohen, Natan Solomon, and Channel 14 reporter Tamir Schneid did not respond to the inquiry. Neither did Gadi Taub or Alon Malik, who were asked if the company pays them or if they pay the company for producing the podcasts.
Haaretz also contacted Yinon Magal, who provided an irrelevant response. Ophir Falk stated that "among the multitude of false claims, the most absurd is that the prime minister's book was written by me. Prime Minister Netanyahu wrote every single word in his book, and the proof of this is the original manuscript kept in his possession." However, a Haaretz inquiry reveals that Netanyahu wrote in his book that Falk typed the content during travels across the country.
The Likud stated in response that the party "legally hired NVP in accordance with all laws for election campaign productions," but the party did not respond to Haaretz's questions regarding the connection between Gross and Netanyahu.

The cost of the plant producing solid rocket fuel for Flamingo missiles in Denmark has become known
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
15:04:49 EEST

The cost of the plant producing solid rocket fuel for Flamingo missiles in Denmark has become known
Kyiv • UNN
The cost of the Fire Point plant in Denmark increased due to the construction of a new facility. Its launch is scheduled by the end of 2027.
The cost of the plant for producing solid rocket propellant for Flamingo missiles, which the Ukrainian company Fire Point is building in Denmark, is estimated at more than €150 million. Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh said this during a press conference at the DALO Industry Days arms exhibition, UNN reports.
"At present, this is a very rough estimate. But the initial plan was to complete the entire project within €50 million. The cost has now risen to more than €150 million," Iryna Terekh said.
According to her, the cost tripled after it became clear that the first building purchased by the company was unsuitable for housing solid rocket propellant production, and the company was forced to build a new facility.
Iryna Terekh also added that Fire Point is already producing rocket propellant in Ukraine.
"But when it came to scaling up production, given the need for predictable capacity located in a safe place, we chose Denmark—or, more precisely, accepted Denmark's very generous invitation to establish such a plant here," she explained.
The CEO of Rocket Technology, a subsidiary of Fire Point, Viacheslav Bondarchuk, added that 100 people are working on the project, 15 of whom are executives and managers, while the rest are contractors. In the future, the company plans to hire several hundred more people for administrative positions, its engineering team, and production.
"Our first and foremost goal is to solve what is, so to speak, a common European problem (…). And we plan to open a plant here (in Denmark—Ed.) that will have enormous capacity to produce large quantities of solid rocket propellant, initially for Fire Point. We will also be able to supply other companies," Bondarchuk said.
According to him, the plant is currently under construction. The company already has all the necessary permits to build the plant and begin producing solid rocket propellant. The plant is scheduled to become operational by the end of 2027.
We remind you
As UNN reported, Fire Point is building a solid rocket propellant plant in the Danish town of Vojens, in the south of the country. This is the first case within NATO in which a member state has allowed a Ukrainian defense company to establish a production site on its territory.
For Fire Point to be able to begin producing solid propellant for Flamingo missiles, the Danish authorities removed more than 20 legislative barriers.
Locating production in Denmark will minimize the risk of a possible Russian strike on the facility.

Seven people, including six tourists and a pilot, were killed on Wednesday when a helicopter crashed at Mount Ololokwe in northern Kenya, according to local media reports citing local officials.
 
The crash occurred at Mount Ololokwe in Samburu County, about 270 kilometers (168 miles) north of the capital Nairobi.
 
Local media, quoting officials in the area, reported that all seven people aboard the helicopter died. The identities and nationalities of the six tourists had not been officially released.
 
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) confirmed the accident but did not provide an official casualty figure in its initial statement.
 
"The Authority extends its deepest condolences to the families of the victims following this tragic incident," the KCAA said Wednesday.
 
The aviation regulator identified the aircraft as a Eurocopter EC130 B4, registration 5Y-GYM. It said the helicopter was flying from Loisaba to Ewasonyiro when it crashed at about 9.13 am local time (0613 GMT) at Mount Ololokwe.
 
The aviation authority said it is coordinating with relevant government agencies and other stakeholders in response to the accident.
 
The Air Accident Investigation Department under Kenya's Roads and Transport Ministry is leading investigations into the circumstances surrounding the crash.
 
Authorities did not immediately disclose the possible cause of the accident.
The area surrounding Mount Ololokwe, also known as Ol Donyo Sabache, forms part of Kenya's northern tourism circuit, which draws international visitors to wildlife reserves and conservancies across the region.
 
Light aircraft and helicopters are widely used to transport tourists between safari lodges, conservancies and other destinations in remote parts of northern Kenya.
 
According to the KCAA, investigators are working to establish the circumstances that led to the crash.

Israel opens criminal probes over killings of Hind Rajab and Gaza rescue workers, military says
JERUSALEM/CAIRO, Aug 19 - Israel's military will open internal investigations over its troops' high-profile killings in Gaza of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in January 2024 and 15 emergency and aid workers in March 2025, it said on Wednesday, although rights groups said such probes rarely lead to convictions.
The military said the investigation decisions followed probes by its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism. It released decisions regarding five incidents involving the deaths of Palestinians.
They included an examination of the killings of seven aid workers with the World Central Kitchen charity in April 2024. On that incident, the military said there was "no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation."
Israeli rights groups say that criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.
Dan Owen, a researcher in the Yesh Din rights organization, said that over the last decade only a "tiny" proportion of investigations had led to indictments while growing political pressure "further deters Israeli law-enforcement authorities from holding those responsible accountable, even when clear evidence does exist."
During Israel's offensive in response to an October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel which triggered the Gaza war, Hind Rajab was pinned down in a car for hours, begging Palestinian medics by mobile phone to send help, while her aunt, uncle and three cousins already lay dead. When an ambulance arrived, contact with the girl and the rescuers themselves was lost. Twelve days later, the bodies of the girl, her relatives and two ambulance workers were recovered from the area.
HIND RAJAB FILM
A film about Hind Rajab's death won the Silver Lion Award at the Venice Film Festival and was nominated for an Academy Award.
In March 2025, 15 emergency and aid workers from the Red Crescent, Palestinian Civil Defense and the United Nations were recovered from a grave in the sand in the south of the Gaza Strip, U.N. officials said at the time.
U.N. aid chief Tom Fletcher said in a post on X that the bodies were buried near "wrecked & well-marked vehicles," adding: "They were killed by Israeli forces while trying to save lives. We demand answers & justice."
Israeli forces say they have never deliberately targeted civilians in the Gaza war. They say the Palestinian militant group Hamas endangers such people's lives by using them for cover.
The Israeli military did not immediately comment directly on the deaths of the Red Crescent workers at the time. In a later statement to Reuters, it said that it had facilitated the evacuation of the bodies from the area, which it described as an active combat zone. It did not specifically respond to questions about why the bodies were retrieved from beneath the sand or why the vehicles were found crushed.
Eid Aziz, media director for the Red Crescent, told Reuters:

Munther Abed, a Palestinian paramedic who said he was present at the incident in which 15 of his colleagues were killed, told Reuters on Wednesday he hoped "those who killed my colleagues, who were like family to me, face justice, real justice".
"I want to say to the whole world, Ambulances 101 is not a target and they must be protected," he said referring to the speed dial number for the Red Crescent Service in Gaza.
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the Gaza war in 2023, with thousands more killed in its military operations in southern Lebanon. The dead include many aid workers, doctors, journalists and others.
Israel's military, which says its attacks target Hamas and Hezbollah militants, opens investigations into some of its attacks, when they involve the deaths of civilians including medical and aid workers or journalists.
The Gaza ceasefire declared in last October may have halted major fighting in Gaza but it failed to end Israeli attacks. Israel has said its ongoing strikes aim to thwart imminent attacks by Hamas and other Gaza militants.

How the use of artificial intelligence harms college students’ ability to learn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:00:43 UTC
21:00:43 KST

College students who copy answers from artificial intelligence tools without verifying the information experience declines in their ability to learn independently. These unreflective habits are associated with a weaker belief in students’ own capabilities and a reduced motivation to learn. The findings were published in Scientific Reports.
Generative artificial intelligence programs can quickly write essays, generate computer code, and solve advanced mathematical equations. These tools have become common academic aids on college campuses across the globe. When students use these systems to seek explanations or brainstorm new ideas, the technology can expand their academic perspectives and improve their studying efficiency.
But reliance on automated answers carries potential academic risks. Hui Zhao and Huijuan Gu, researchers at Zhoukou Normal University, designed a study to examine what happens when students use artificial intelligence thoughtlessly. The researchers define thoughtless use as a pattern in which users blindly adopt machine-generated text without critically evaluating, verifying, or deeply understanding the outputs.
The researchers wanted to know how this specific habit affects self-directed learning. Self-directed learning is a core educational skill in higher education. It refers to a student’s capacity to independently set goals, apply study strategies, and monitor their own academic progress. Students with high self-directed learning abilities can manage their time and actively evaluate what they do and do not understand.
To understand the relationship between technology habits and study skills, the researchers looked at two psychological factors. The first is self-efficacy, which is a person’s internal belief in their capacity to successfully complete tasks and overcome challenges. The second factor is learning motivation, which encompasses the psychological drives that push a student to initiate and persist in their coursework. The researchers based their investigation on the idea that a student’s environment, personal beliefs, and daily behaviors all shape one another in a continuous, reciprocal cycle.
Zhao and Gu recruited 487 undergraduate students from four universities in Henan Province, China, to complete an online survey. The participants answered a series of questions assessing their study habits on a five-point scale. The respondents ranged from college freshmen to seniors and represented a variety of academic disciplines, including the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences.
The survey measured four distinct categories using established psychological scales. First, it assessed how often students engaged in thoughtless artificial intelligence use. Participants rated their agreement with statements such as “I copy learning tasks or problem statements into generative AI to seek answers or ideas” and “I feel that generative AI is more capable than I am in learning and problem-solving.”
Second, the survey measured the students’ academic self-efficacy. This section asked participants to reflect on their confidence when facing difficult materials, using prompts like “I believe that I can independently master complex learning content.”
Third, the researchers measured the students’ overall motivation to learn. This included questions about their curiosity, their desire to master new skills, and the satisfaction they gained from overcoming academic hurdles. Finally, the survey evaluated the students’ capacity for self-directed learning by asking how often they actively checked their own understanding of the material or created knowledge frameworks like mind maps.
The researchers used a statistical technique called structural equation modeling to analyze the survey responses. This analytical method allows scientists to observe complex networks of relationships between multiple different variables at the same time, rather than just looking at two variables in isolation.
The analysis revealed that the thoughtless use of artificial intelligence is strongly associated with lower levels of self-directed learning. Students who habitually relied on automated answers reported worse self-management skills and lower cognitive engagement in their coursework.
The researchers identified a specific psychological pathway explaining this decline. The authors suggest that an unreflective reliance on technology deprives students of the opportunity to struggle through complex problems. Without the experience of overcoming academic challenges through their own hard work, students reported lower levels of self-efficacy.
This lower confidence in their own abilities was in turn linked to a reduced motivation to learn. When individuals do not believe they can succeed on their own, their willingness to invest effort naturally declines. With less motivation and lower self-confidence, the students became less capable of managing their own educational progress, acting instead as dependent users of external tools.
The researchers also conducted a multi-group analysis to see if these patterns differed between men and women. This statistical test allowed the authors to compare the strength of the psychological relationships across the two demographic groups.
The analysis uncovered distinct gender differences in how thoughtless technology use relates to psychological well-being. For male students, unreflective use showed a stronger negative association with learning motivation. The researchers suggest that male students often view technology primarily as a tool for efficiency, meaning that immediate automated answers quickly replace their internal drive to engage deeply with the material.
For female students, thoughtless use was associated with steeper declines in self-efficacy and self-directed learning. The researchers note that female students tend to adopt more reflective and evaluative study strategies in their traditional coursework. When they bypass these reflective processes by copying automated answers, they miss out on the mastery experiences that traditionally build their academic confidence.
The study relies on cross-sectional data, meaning all the information was collected at a single point in time. Because the researchers did not track the students over a long period, the statistical results highlight relationships between behaviors and beliefs but cannot definitively prove cause and effect. It is possible that students who already have low self-efficacy are simply more likely to use artificial intelligence thoughtlessly.
The demographic makeup of the sample also presents some limitations. The participants were drawn exclusively from universities in a single Chinese province, and nearly eighty percent of the respondents were female. Expanding future surveys to include a more balanced demographic distribution across different regions would help verify if these patterns hold true for other student populations.
Additionally, the survey measured motivation as a single, unified concept. Future research could split this category into intrinsic motivation, such as natural curiosity, and extrinsic motivation, such as a desire for good grades. Separating these concepts would provide a more detailed picture of how automated tools influence a student’s inner drive to succeed. Future studies might also track students over an entire semester to see how their habits and self-confidence evolve as they face different types of academic challenges.
The study, “Thoughtless Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence and College Students’ Self-Directed Learning: A Multi-Group SEM Analysis of Gender Differences,” was authored by Hui Zhao and Huijuan Gu.
